Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Registration for Riaan Manser's Antarctica expeditions is now open.

Unique Selling Point:
Antarctica: A land of frigidity, moisture, and aridity. Temperatures can plummet to a bone-chilling -60°C, a paradise for researchers. Here, the chronicles of our planet rest undisturbed, locked within the frozen embrace of ice.

Riaan Manser seeks out five ambitious high school students for a transformative odyssey.

Amidst the backdrop of escalating global temperatures, triggering the dissolution of Antarctic ice and the consequent surge in sea levels, this expedition promises profound revelations.

During this fully funded expedition, these students will imbibe priceless wisdom, igniting an inner fire. Enthused to galvanize their local communities, they will emerge as champions of a more luminous future—for themselves, their progeny, and the very Earth we share.

Summary:
Riaan Manser, an experienced explorer in his fourth year of Antarctic expeditions, is extending an invitation to five South African high school students. They have the incredible opportunity to join him on a fully funded expedition to Antarctica.

This exceptional and unparalleled experience provides students with the chance to deepen their understanding of how global warming affects our everyday existence.

Engaging in hands-on experiments and activities, participants will create lasting memories and gain invaluable insights.

Visuals: Earth from space (NASA Footage)
VO 1: In the vastness of the universe, this celestial sphere serves as our precious home: Planet Earth.

But our sanctuary is under threat.

For decades, scientists have been sounding the alarm about the dangers of global warming and climate change. And in recent years, we’ve seen for ourselves the increasing unpredictability and severity of…. floods…Wildfires and droughts.

Visuals: Carte Blanche January 2023 Archive footage
VO2: It’s a global crisis. And we may have passed the tipping point. This is the continent which is the barometer of man’s impact on the environment. Welcome to Antarctica!

Visuals: Carte Blanche January 2023 Archive footage
VO3: Explorer Riaan Manser is embarking on his fourth mission to Antarctic, and he’s seeking five grade 11 students to join him on this once-in-a-lifetime expedition.
Visuals: Thea cellphone footage
VO4: Scan the QR code on your screen to enter the Matrics in Antarctica competition, or dive into social our social media pages for more information. Entries close on the 30th of September.

Don't hesitate—take the plunge into this unparalleled experience.

TX 11 February 2024
CARTE BLANCHE
Matrics in Antarctica 2023
Insert Script

JAMES:
It’s the coldest place on the planet.

DIMAKATSO:
It’s the largest and driest desert on earth.

KEIRA:
It shows humanity’s insignificance and nature’s grandeur.

SIBAHLE:
It’s breathtaking.

CHLOE:
A beauty that will stay with you for the rest of your life.

MASA:
THIS, is Anttarctica

CHLOE:
My name is Chloe Diederichs-Boudouris.
I entered for this experience because I want to see what I can do to positively impact the planet, and how I can encourage other people to do the same.

DIMAKATSO:
I'm Dimakatso Seriti
I've always wanted to go to space, but now that I'm in Antarctica, I get to learn about the environment and how we impact it.

JAMES:
I’m James Pringle.
I want to be as sustainable as possible. I can make a difference by going paperless myself and doing work in my local community to really aid in sustainability.

SIBAHLE:
I'm Sibahle Fetile. I'm from a small rural town situated in the Eastern Cape.
I'm hoping to get the experience of the life, the landscape, the environment…

KEIRA:
My name is Kara King.
Going to Antarctica means that I'll come back with stories to share to the youth, to make sure that they can make a change too.

MASA:
For the past four years Riaan Manser has been bringing five matrics to this white continent believing that educating and empowering the youth, can make a difference.

MASA
Manser, a veteran adventurer and environmentalist, knows getting people, especially the youth, excited about the environment, can be quite a challenge.

RIAAN:
Taking five matric students, we take them to Antarctica, and we try to find the next environmental rock star…
You have to make it attractive for young people. You can't have this mature concept and idea that is so many layers thick.
We need to convince the millions that saving the environment is for their good, and it's actually something they practically can do.
Okay, this is cold for real…

MASA:
Today’s youth are arguably more environmentally aware than past generations. Many manage to mould their interests and beliefs into passion projects that bring about change.

Chloe, a sports fanatic, chose to re-direct her energies into serving on the Jo'burg Junior Council's Environmental Committee.

CHLOE
I'm really passionate about the environment. And it's actually been such an incredible experience because we've worked with the SPCA, we've done a recycled runway where we've had Greenpeace Africa as a guest speaker.
We've really just done so much to try and benefit out and like, uplift our community as much as we can.

DIMAKATSO:
If we really want to educate people about and push for more climate action, we really need to start telling people how it affects them, because only then do they really care.

MASA:
Becoming environmentally aware these days is as much about seeing the world around us, as it is what we learn from books. James…… was deeply impacted by the drought in the Western Cape in 2016 and 2017.


JAMES:
Climate change is real. There's something that is wrong and there's something that needs to be done. And I think in Antarctica, seeing that effect happen effectively in real time at an insane rate… it'll help to validate that feeling that, you know, we need to do something.


SIBAHLE:
Since I'm in love with science, how do I say to myself, like, we must bring innovative ideas to make the environment more conducive, more sustainable.

MASA:
For his science project, Sibahle turned to nuclear power… more specifically, the waste generated…
His research led him to microorganisms that show resistance to radiation.

SIBAHLE:
They are able to consume the metals. They can extract the electrons from their metals while consuming them, producing an electric current that can be used to produce electricity.

MASA:
For Keira, though, environmental issues are much closer to home…

KEIRA:
I'm in the water and on the beach a lot. And especially in Durban, we have lots of problems with litter on our beaches and the e-coli levels.

When the oceans are unhappy, I feel unhappy. So my passion for the ocean made me feel like I needed to make a difference.

MASA:
So she reached out to SANCCOB, The Foundation for the Conservation of Coastal Birds.

KEIRA:
Penguins are indicator species. So if the oceans unhealthy, then the numbers of those animals will drop.

MASA:
To raise funds for SANCCOB and its vital African Penguin programme she paddled - with her hands - from Ballito to Durban on a prone board…

KEIRA:
So initially we thought it was going to be 40 K's. And then during my paddle it was all good. And then we reached the Umgeni mouth and I clocked 40 and I still had to get to the harbour wall. And I was thinking, oh my gosh…

MASA:
Antarctica is also home to penguins. In fact it’s the only place on earth where Emperor penguins breed in the wild.
Marine Scientist, Maryke Musson, has been a Matrics in Antarctica expedition lead from the outset. She’s also the brains behind the Human-Penguin Waddle involving a run or jog throughout the night to raise money for SANCCOB.

MARYKE:
Yes, we managed to rake up the kilometres and I think collectively we must have done well over 150 kms, but individually every student contributed. They were the real stars.

JAMES:
Who really needs sleep, am I right? It’s to raise funds for SANCCOB.

CHLOE:
I managed to do 21 K's, and it was just really it was really special just to be able to do that and know that you're making a big impact from the small little thing that you're busy doing.

MASA:
Antarctica has experienced air temperature increases 5 times higher than the mean rate of global warming. Studying what happens here, enables scientists to more accurately predict future climate change.

MASA:
Absolutely incredible. Right now, I’m standing in an actual glacier. We’ve been hiking and we’ve gone through and inside a glacier. Ice, snow everywhere. It’s absolutely beautiful. Also known, informally, as, the ice tunnels.

JAMES:
It was incredibly surreal and coming out in the other side, it was absolutely gorgeous. I mean, you could see the sun kind of shining over the hills and it was it was insane. I loved it.

DIMAKATSO
All this time I had been learning about the environment and how we are affected, but this time it was me actually coming here and seeing the beauty of this place. Seeing how much learning we can get from just this one place.

KEIRA:
The first step on the ice was also really amazing because it was so different to what I thought.
So going through the ice tunnel, the colors of blue were amazing. And just being in that space where the topography is so different to what I expected.

SIBAHLE:
My favorite part of the Antarctica is the sun that never sets. It's surreal. Like, it feels like I'm in another planet.

MASA:
What’s been your highlight for this particular trip?

RIAAN:
Creating something and it's not just in the in the form of these five coming together and talking about the environment and hopefully planning to make change. What we actually did was put up a solar system that is going to make change in this base, in this camp that hasn't had any green energy for over 20 years.

MASA:
The matrics rolled up their sleeves and helped install a system that, if replicated across a few more of these containers, would make it possible to switch off the generators for good.

(PAUSE) Once installed, it was down to yours truly to flick the switch from generator to solar power.

MASA:
I’m about to switch the light on and make history!

MASA:
And our five matrics, are geared up to go and change the world to preserve a healthier, happier planet, for generations to come.

RIAAN:
You have 200,000 people that are visiting the continent right now, but like less than 1% visit deep field Antarctica and this is where these students come. They are going to sit in boardrooms where people are going to be waxing lyrical about their knowledge about the environment, and not one of them would have gone to Antarctica, except that student. There's some power in there.

DIMAKATSO:
I just have a new fire in me, and I can't wait to go out there and tell my story of Antarctica and how beautiful it is, and how we really need to protect the ecosystem here, just from our own homes.

MASA:
It’s past 8pm and the sun is shining bright as ever, because it’s summer in Antarctica. Let me tell you, it is freezing, but I am layered up and layered up but enjoying the sun. As much as I thought I was prepared for the 24 hour daylight, when it’s sleeping time, it kind of messes with you mind a bit. But what a treat. What a magnificent place to be in. And whatever the expectations that I had about being here, have been far exceeded.

MASA:
And like the rest of our planet… it’s a place worth saving..

DIMAKATSO All this time I had been learning about the environment and how we are affected, but this time it was me actually coming here and seeing the beauty of this place. Seeing how much learning we can get from just this one place. KEIRA: The first step on the ice was also really amazing because it was so different to what I thought. So going through the ice tunnel, the colors of blue were amazing. And just being in that space where the topography is so different to what I expected. SIBAHLE: My favorite part of the Antarctica is the sun that never sets. It's surreal. Like, it feels like I'm in another planet. MASA: What’s been your highlight for this particular trip? RIAAN: Creating something and it's not just in the in the form of these five coming together and talking about the environment and hopefully planning to make change. What we actually did was put up a solar system that is going to make change in this base, in this camp that hasn't had any green energy for over 20 years. MASA: The matrics rolled up their sleeves and helped install a system that, if replicated across a few more of these containers, would make it possible to switch off the generators for good. (PAUSE) Once installed, it was down to yours truly to flick the switch from generator to solar power. MASA: I’m about to switch the light on and make history! MASA: And our five matrics, are geared up to go and change the world to preserve a healthier, happier planet, for generations to come. RIAAN: You have 200,000 people that are visiting the continent right now, but like less than 1% visit deep field Antarctica and this is where these students come. They are going to sit in boardrooms where people are going to be waxing lyrical about their knowledge about the environment, and not one of them would have gone to Antarctica, except that student. There's some power in there. DIMAKATSO: I just have a new fire in me, and I can't wait to go out there and tell my story of Antarctica and how beautiful it is, and how we really need to protect the ecosystem here, just from our own homes. MASA: It’s past 8pm and the sun is shining bright as ever, because it’s summer in Antarctica. Let me tell you, it is freezing, but I am layered up and layered up but enjoying the sun. As much as I thought I was prepared for the 24 hour daylight, when it’s sleeping time, it kind of messes with you mind a bit. But what a treat. What a magnificent place to be in. And whatever the expectations that I had about being here, have been far exceeded. MASA: And like the rest of our planet… it’s a place worth saving..

metadata.Unique Selling Point: Antarctica: A land of frigidity, moisture, and aridity. Temperatures can plummet to a bone-chilling -60°C, a paradise for researchers. Here, the chronicles of our planet rest undisturbed, locked within the frozen embrace of ice. Riaan Manser seeks out five ambitious high school students for a transformative odyssey. Amidst the backdrop of escalating global temperatures, triggering the dissolution of Antarctic ice and the consequent surge in sea levels, this expedition promises profound revelations. During this fully funded expedition, these students will imbibe priceless wisdom, igniting an inner fire. Enthused to galvanize their local communities, they will emerge as champions of a more luminous future—for themselves, their progeny, and the very Earth we share.
metadata.Summary: Riaan Manser, an experienced explorer in his fourth year of Antarctic expeditions, is extending an invitation to five South African high school students. They have the incredible opportunity to join him on a fully funded expedition to Antarctica. This exceptional and unparalleled experience provides students with the chance to deepen their understanding of how global warming affects our everyday existence. Engaging in hands-on experiments and activities, participants will create lasting memories and gain invaluable insights.
